notes: MHRT apparent bias appeal; Article 6 and Rule 8(2) analysis are clear and the appeal was dismissed.

enrichment.short_title: MHRT medical member employed by detaining Trust: no apparent bias
key_facts: Patient D was detained under section 3 of the Mental Health Act 1983 at Rathbone Hospital, part of Mersey Care NHS Trust.
The Mental Health Review Tribunal dismissed his discharge application; the medical member Dr Izmeth was employed by the Trust at the Hesketh Centre in a different clinical directorate.
D sought judicial review on apparent bias grounds; Silber J dismissed the claim and D appealed with permission.
Dr Izmeth had no prior dealings with D, the RMO, witnesses, or Rathbone Hospital other than as a tribunal member.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from judicial review refusing to quash a Mental Health Review Tribunal decision on apparent bias grounds.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; no real possibility of apparent bias where a Trust-employed consultant sat on the tribunal given the safeguards and factual separation between directorates.
enrichment.ratio: There is no general rule that an employee of a party to tribunal proceedings can never sit without apparent bias; the fair-minded observer test from Porter v Magill and Lawal applies, and Rule 8(2)(b) of the 1983 Rules does not disqualify a consultant psychiatrist who is not a managerial officer of the health authority.
legal_issues: Whether Dr Izmeth was disqualified by apparent bias as a Trust employee
Construction of 'officer' in Rule 8(2)(b) of the Mental Health Review Tribunal Rules 1983
Whether the Conflict of Interest Guidelines demonstrated a risk of bias
Whether safeguards comparable to R v Spear could exclude apparent bias

Porter v Magill [2002] 2 AC 357
R v Spear [2003] 1 AC 734
Findlay v United Kingdom (1997) 24 EHRR 221
Aerts v Belgium (1998) 29 EHRR 50
Johnson v Johnson [2000] 200 CLR 488

notes: Agassi sports endorsement tax appeal; sections 555-556 ICTA 1988 construction and territorial principle analysis are straightforward.

enrichment.short_title: Non-resident sportsman's UK endorsement income under section 556
key_facts: André Agassi, a US-resident tennis player, received endorsement payments from Nike and Head via his US company for UK tournament activities.
The Revenue assessed additional tax on connected payments; the Special Commissioners dismissed Agassi's appeal.
Agassi argued section 556(5) precluded assessment where the foreign payers had no UK tax presence and section 555(2) did not apply.
Payments were connected with relevant sporting activities performed in the United Kingdom.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal from a Special Commissioners' decision on income tax assessments for 1998/1999.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; section 555(2) applies to payments by foreign companies with no UK tax presence, so section 556(5) does not exclude Agassi's liability.
enrichment.ratio: In the context of anti-avoidance provisions extending Schedule D charge on non-resident sportsmen, section 555(2) imposes obligations on payers irrespective of UK tax presence; it would be absurd if liability could be avoided simply by channelling payments through foreign companies with no UK presence.
legal_issues: Whether section 556 applies where payments are made by foreign companies with no UK tax presence
Construction of section 556(5) and its linkage to section 555(2)
Application of the territorial principle from Clark v Oceanic Contractors
Whether attribution of income to Agassi under section 556(2) is precluded
linked_authorities: Clark v Oceanic Contractors 56 TC 183
Colquhoun v Brooks (1889) 14 App Cas 493
Cooke v Charles A Vogeler Company [1901] AC 192

confidence.notes: Single issue of statutory construction with clear reasoning. Factual payment figures are secondary to the legal question.

notes: Solicitor commission contract and Consumer Credit Act preliminary issue; credit/not-credit distinction and costs ruling are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Solicitor commission advances not regulated credit under CCA 1974
key_facts: Sarah Range joined McMillan Williams as an assistant solicitor on a commission-only contract with monthly advances of £22,000 per annum.
Her billing fell well below the benchmark needed to cover advances; on resignation the firm claimed about £18,333 for the shortfall plus interest.
Range argued the contract was an unenforceable regulated agreement under the Consumer Credit Act 1974.
A preliminary issue was tried at Brighton County Court; the judge found for Range and the firm appealed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a preliminary issue determining whether an employment commission contract was a regulated consumer credit agreement.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the contract was not regulated credit and was enforceable; each party to bear its own costs of the Court of Appeal.
enrichment.ratio: Where it is completely uncertain at contract formation whether arrangements will give rise to a debt, there is no 'credit' merely because payment is deferred until a future calculation crystallises; monthly advances on anticipated commission are remuneration, not financial accommodation.
legal_issues: Whether monthly commission advances constituted 'credit' under section 9 of the Consumer Credit Act 1974
Whether the agreement was a regulated agreement exceeding £25,000 or an exempt agreement
Application of Goode's ingredients of credit and Dimond v Lovell
Appropriate costs order where ADR was recommended but mediation failed

notes: Kosovo asylum Article 8 JR; Shala delay principles and IAT leave refusal review are detailed and the claim failed clearly.

enrichment.short_title: Kosovan asylum seeker's Article 8 JR after IAT refused leave
key_facts: Ethnic Albanian claimant from Kosovo arrived in the UK in July 1998 and claimed asylum; his claim was refused in July 2001 after Home Office delay.
He established a private life in Cardiff as a taxi driver and court interpreter but had no family life in the UK.
The adjudicator found Article 8 interference but held removal proportionate; the IAT refused leave to appeal.
The claimant argued the adjudicator failed properly to apply Shala on delay and legitimate initial asylum claim.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Immigration Appeal Tribunal's refusal of leave to appeal an adjudicator's dismissal of an Article 8 appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; permission to appeal refused; no order as to costs.
enrichment.ratio: The Shala delay point requires all three preconditions and has little application outside marriage-type cases; where only private life is engaged, delay is a relevant but rarely decisive factor, and the adjudicator's proportionality balancing was within the permissible range.
legal_issues: Whether the IAT erred in refusing leave to appeal on Article 8 grounds
Application of Arben Shala v SSHD on Home Office delay and proportionality
Whether the adjudicator adequately considered legitimate initial claim and delay
Distinction between private life and family life under Article 8
linked_authorities: Arben Shala v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2003] EWCA Civ 233

notes: False imprisonment and malicious prosecution after Chris Alder death; jury withdrawal issues are extensively reasoned and appeal allowed.

enrichment.short_title: False imprisonment and malicious prosecution after custody death

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994

key_facts: Jason Paul intervened in a fight outside a Hull club; Chris Alder later died in police custody after being arrested at hospital.
Paul voluntarily attended the police station, was arrested for murder, later charged with GBH with intent, and detained overnight before magistrates granted bail.
Proceedings were discontinued in July 1998; Paul claimed false imprisonment and malicious prosecution.
At trial the judge directed judgment for the police, holding no factual issues remained for the jury on good faith and reasonable cause.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a county court judge's directed verdict at the end of a jury trial in false imprisonment and malicious prosecution claims.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; retrial ordered before judge and jury; defendant to pay claimant's costs of the appeal.
enrichment.ratio: There was evidence for the jury on whether arrest discretion was exercised in good faith, whether charging lacked honest belief in unlawful conduct despite objective reasonable cause, and whether bail refusal was motivated by improper distraction from the custody death; the judge wrongly withdrew these issues.
legal_issues: Whether arrest under PACE section 24(6) was exercised in good faith
Subjective and objective elements of malicious prosecution under Glinski v McIver

notes: Employment tribunal bias and costs appeal; EAT jurisdiction and contributory fault on costs are clearly resolved.

enrichment.short_title: Employment tribunal chairman recusal and costs order quashed

statutes_considered.title: Employment Tribunals (Constitution and Rules of Procedure) Regulations 2001

key_facts: Rodrigo Lodwick, appearing in person, asked Employment Tribunal chairman Mr Peters to recuse himself because of adverse comments in a 1998 case where Lodwick had represented another claimant against Southwark.
The tribunal refused recusal and after a five-day hearing dismissed unfair dismissal and breach claims, ordering Lodwick to pay £4,000 costs.
The EAT held it had no jurisdiction because the bias allegation lacked substance.
Mummery LJ granted permission to appeal on the unusual bias and costs features.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against Employment Appeal Tribunal decision declining jurisdiction over bias challenge and upholding a costs order.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; case remitted to the EAT on bias; £4,000 costs order quashed at this stage.
enrichment.ratio: An allegation of apparent bias based on prior adverse comments about a representative in an earlier case against the same respondent was not so lacking in substance as to deprive the EAT of jurisdiction; the 'equal vote of three members' reason was weak, and the costs order lacked sufficient clarity and proper application of the exceptional costs test.

notes: Colombian asylum appeal on new FARC evidence; E and R mistake-of-fact and Ladd v Marshall analysis is thorough.

enrichment.short_title: Colombian asylum appeal: new FARC evidence rejected

statutes_considered.title: Geneva Convention relating to the Status of Refugees 1951

key_facts: Colombian husband and wife fled after extortion linked to refusal to pay FARC-related demands following involvement in a neighbourhood association.
The adjudicator found honest witnesses but held they fled general insecurity and simple extortion, not Convention persecution.
On appeal the IAT dismissed the appeal; new FARC documents from 2003 were later said to have been omitted from IAT bundles.
Fresh evidence included a FARC public announcement, police reports, and a newspaper article about kidnapping of the association president.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal against IAT dismissal and against failure to set aside the determination under Rule 30(2)(c).
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on both grounds; no order as to costs.
enrichment.ratio: New material did not establish an established relevant mistake of fact under E and R, failed Ladd v Marshall on diligence and materiality, and did not justify setting aside the IAT determination; non-renewal principles from Horvath on state protection also undermined the claim.
legal_issues: Whether mistake of fact giving rise to unfairness can found a point of law appeal under E and R
Admissibility of fresh evidence under Ladd v Marshall in asylum appeals

notes: London Underground unfair dismissal; range of reasonable responses and disciplinary charge framing are clearly analysed.

enrichment.short_title: Tube driver's unfair dismissal over Belgium line car trip
key_facts: Michael Strouthos, a tube train driver of 20 years, used a company Ford Mondeo to drive colleagues to a shooting trip in Belgium in September 2001.
Customs impounded cigarettes and alcohol on return; no charges were brought and the vehicle was returned after two months.
He was dismissed for gross misconduct including taking the car abroad without permission and reputational damage; the ET found unfair dismissal with 20% contributory fault.
The EAT reversed, holding dismissal was within the band of reasonable responses and contributory fault should be 51%.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against Employment Appeal Tribunal decision substituting a finding that dismissal was fair.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; Employment Tribunal decision restored; 20% contributory fault upheld; appellant awarded costs.
enrichment.ratio: The EAT erred in treating breach of trust as automatically justifying dismissal as a matter of law and in finding the ET's conclusion perverse; the ET was entitled to find dismissal outside the range of reasonable responses where the Customs episode was not gross misconduct and the formal charge did not allege initial dishonesty in taking the car.
legal_issues: Whether dismissal was within the range of reasonable responses under section 98(4)
Application of British Home Stores v Burchell and Foley v Post Office
Whether disciplinary charge framing limited findings of dishonesty
Appropriate contributory fault percentage

notes: Inheritance tax negligence limitation issue; Forster line and White v Jones analogy are extensively analysed.

enrichment.short_title: IHT reservation-of-benefit advice: limitation in solicitor negligence
key_facts: Mrs Daniels transferred Thornfield to her son by deed of gift in August 1989 on solicitor advice but continued living there rent-free until her death in 1998.
Section 102 Finance Act 1986 reservation-of-benefit rules brought Thornfield back into the estate; inheritance tax of £30,980.80 was paid.
The executor son sued the solicitor for negligent failure to advise on reservation of benefit.
A preliminary issue was tried on when the cause of action accrued and whether limitation barred the claim.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from preliminary issue on limitation in professional negligence claim for inheritance tax loss.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; tort claim time-barred; application to amend to plead duty owed to personal representative refused.
enrichment.ratio: Assuming a cause of action in negligence, Mrs Daniels suffered loss when she entered the ineffective PET in August 1989 under the Forster principle; the pleaded IHT liability was not loss she personally could suffer, and no viable cause of action vested in the personal representative under section 1(1) of the 1934 Act.
legal_issues: When damage accrues in professional negligence affecting inheritance tax planning
Whether reservation-of-benefit IHT liability is loss suffered by the testator or the estate
Application of Forster v Outred and White v Jones principles
Whether a personal representative can maintain an alternative negligence claim

notes: Commercial agents regulation 18(a) construction; distinction from Light v Ty Europe is clearly reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Commercial agent compensation when contract expires by effluxion
key_facts: Three long-serving agents for Pure Fishing held six-monthly agency contracts for Abu Garcia, Berkley and Fenwick brands expiring on 30 June 1999.
Pure Fishing introduced Abu Garcia floats and swim-feeders conflicting with the agents' Drennan agency; agents refused to sell the new products.
On 16 June 1999 Pure Fishing wrote that it would not enter new contracts, citing material breach including refusal to sell specified products.
Contracts expired by effluxion of time; agents claimed compensation under regulation 17.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Mercantile Court judgment on entitlement to compensation under the Commercial Agents Regulations 1993.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; regulation 18(a) did not exclude compensation where the principal simply allowed contracts to expire without renewal.
enrichment.ratio: Regulation 18(a) requires the principal unilaterally to terminate the agency contract because of agent default justifying immediate termination under regulation 16; deciding not to renew when a fixed-term contract expires is not 'termination' for that purpose, even though regulation 17 compensation applies on expiry by effluxion of time.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'the principal has terminated' in regulation 18(a)
Relationship between regulation 17 and regulation 18
Whether non-renewal after effluxion of time excludes compensation
Whether agent default justified immediate termination under regulation 16
